stem: A 6-year-old girl has breast development and vaginal bleeding. Serum LH and FSH are low, estradiol and inhibin are markedly high, and pelvic imaging shows a solid ovarian mass.
oneliner: 6F + breast development + vaginal bleeding + low LH/FSH + very high estradiol and inhibin + solid ovarian mass → which cell type?
ask: From which cell type did this tumor most likely arise?

whyNot.A: Make **androgens** and cause virilization, not **breast development with high estradiol**
whyNot.B: Give **dysgerminoma, teratoma or yolk sac** tumors; they do not make **estrogen and inhibin**
whyNot.C: Gives **serous or mucinous** tumors, usually in older women, that do not make **estrogen**
whyNot.E: Give an **ovarian fibroma**, which makes **no estrogen or inhibin**

why: Low gonadotropins with high estrogen from an ovarian mass means **gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty** from a **granulosa cell tumor**, a **sex cord-stromal tumor**. Granulosa cells contain **aromatase**, which makes estrogen, and also secrete **inhibin**, a tumor marker.

idea.rule: Granulosa cell tumor = sex cord-stromal tumor that makes estrogen (aromatase) and inhibin.
also: Causes precocious puberty in girls and postmenopausal bleeding in older women
Raised estrogen predisposes to endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma
Call-Exner bodies are typical of the adult type
Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors instead make androgens (virilization)

stem: A 61-year-old man has erectile dysfunction and is prescribed sildenafil. The drug raises cGMP in the smooth muscle of the paired dorsal erectile bodies of the penis, each of which contains a deep artery.
oneliner: 61M + erectile dysfunction + sildenafil + paired dorsal erectile bodies with deep artery → which structure?
ask: Which penile structure is the main site of the drug's effect?

whyNot.A: Single ventral body around the **urethra** and glans; it does not provide the paired rigid shaft
whyNot.B: A **drainage vessel**; erection depends on filling and compressing its tributaries
whyNot.D: A **fibrous sheath** that compresses emissary veins; it has no smooth muscle to relax
whyNot.E: A **drainage vessel** for the skin; it is not a site of drug action

why: Parasympathetic **NO release** raises **cGMP** and relaxes the **helicine arteries and trabecular smooth muscle** of the paired **corpora cavernosa**, filling them with blood from the **deep artery**. **PDE5 inhibitors** prevent cGMP breakdown in this tissue.

idea.rule: Erection = nitric oxide, cGMP, smooth muscle relaxation in the corpora cavernosa.
also: Sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil: PDE5 inhibitors
Contraindicated with nitrates (severe hypotension)
Priapism: prolonged cavernosal filling

stem: A 24-year-old man has a soft left scrotal mass above the testis that feels like a bag of worms. It enlarges when he stands or performs the Valsalva maneuver. Doppler ultrasound shows reversed venous flow.
oneliner: 24M + soft left scrotal mass above testis + bag of worms + enlarges on standing and Valsalva + reversed venous flow → which vessel?

whyNot.A: An **artery**; it would not fill further on standing or Valsalva or show **reversed venous flow**
whyNot.B: A small **artery** in the cord that does not form a compressible venous mass
whyNot.C: A small **artery** accompanying the vas; it does not dilate to form a mass
whyNot.E: Runs in the **anterior abdominal wall**, not in the spermatic cord

why: A **varicocele** is dilation of the **pampiniform plexus**, the venous network of the spermatic cord. It is usually **left-sided** because the left gonadal vein joins the **left renal vein** at a right angle, and it fills when standing or straining.

idea.rule: Varicocele = dilated cord veins, worse upright, usually left.
also: Left gonadal vein drains to left renal vein; right drains to IVC
Associated with infertility and a smaller testis
Sudden new left varicocele: look for renal vein obstruction

stem: A 45-year-old man with nephrotic-range proteinuria and leg edema develops a new left scrotal varicocele that enlarges on straining. He also has left flank pain and hematuria. The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein.
oneliner: 45M + nephrotic syndrome + new left varicocele + flank pain + hematuria → renal vein sits between which two vessels?
ask: A thrombus in the left renal vein at its crossing lies between which two structures?

options.C: Superior mesenteric artery and celiac trunk
options.D: Left renal artery and left ureter
options.E: Superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein

whyNot.A: The left renal vein passes **in front of the aorta** to reach the IVC, not between these two vessels
whyNot.C: Both are **arteries** off the aorta; the left renal vein does not cross between them
whyNot.D: At the hilum the vein lies **in front of** the renal artery, with the ureter behind and below; the vein does not run between them
whyNot.E: They join to form the **portal vein**, which is not related to the left renal vein

answer: Between the aorta (behind) and the superior mesenteric artery (in front)
why: The **left renal vein** passes **between the aorta and the SMA** before entering the IVC. Nephrotic syndrome is **hypercoagulable**, so **renal vein thrombosis** raises pressure in the **left gonadal vein**, causing the **left varicocele**.

idea.rule: Left-sided only: the left gonadal vein enters the left renal vein, while the right one enters the IVC.
also: Nutcracker syndrome: left renal vein squeezed between aorta and SMA
Nephrotic syndrome: loss of antithrombin III
Right-sided varicocele: look for IVC obstruction

stem: A 64-year-old man undergoes abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, and the left testicular artery is ligated at its origin. Postoperatively, his left testis remains warm and viable on Doppler ultrasound.
oneliner: 64M + AAA repair + left testicular artery ligated + testis stays viable → which collateral artery?
ask: Which artery most likely maintains the testis?

whyNot.A: Branch of the **internal pudendal**; it supplies **scrotal skin**, not the testis itself
whyNot.B: Supplies the **medial thigh**, with no branches to the cord
whyNot.C: A **femoral branch** to the skin over the iliac crest
whyNot.D: A **femoral branch** to the skin of the scrotum, not the testis

answer: Artery of the ductus deferens (with the cremasteric artery)
why: The testis has dual supply. The **testicular artery** comes from the aorta below the renal arteries, and the **artery of the ductus deferens** (a vesical branch of the **internal iliac**) runs with the vas and anastomoses with it. The **cremasteric artery** (inferior epigastric) also helps.

idea.rule: Collateral supply to the testis comes from the internal iliac and inferior epigastric systems.
also: Testicular artery: aorta below the renal arteries
Cremasteric artery: inferior epigastric
Ovary has a similar anastomosis: ovarian and uterine arteries

stem: A 35-year-old woman is evaluated for infertility. During hysterosalpingography, contrast injected through the cervix fills the uterine cavity and both normal-caliber tubes, then spills freely around the bowel loops. She has no pain or bleeding.
oneliner: 35F + infertility workup + HSG contrast fills uterus and both tubes + free spill around bowel + no pain → what does it mean?

whyNot.B: Would cause **acute pain and bleeding**, and the tube would be abnormal
whyNot.C: Contrast would leak from the **uterine body** with pain; here the **uterine cavity and tubes are outlined intact**
whyNot.D: The spill is **real peritoneal contrast** outlining bowel loops, not a technical error
whyNot.E: A **dilated, blocked tube** shows **no free spill**; the tubes here are normal caliber

why: The **fimbriated end** of each fallopian tube **opens into the peritoneal cavity**, so contrast flowing through a patent tube **spills into the peritoneum**. This is a **normal result** that proves the tubes are open.

idea.rule: In women, the peritoneal cavity communicates with the outside world through the tubes, uterus and vagina.
also: Hydrosalpinx: dilated blocked tube without spill
Pelvic inflammatory disease can block the tubes and stop the spill
Gonorrhea or chlamydia can climb through the tubes to cause peritonitis and perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis)

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a left oophorectomy for a 5-cm ovarian mass. The surgeon clamps and divides the suspensory ligament, which carries the ovarian artery and vein over the pelvic brim.
oneliner: 35F + left oophorectomy + suspensory ligament with ovarian vessels divided → structure at risk?
ask: Which structure is most at risk of injury at this step?

whyNot.A: Lies **deeper on the pelvic sidewall**, not in the suspensory ligament
whyNot.B: Crosses the ureter lower, in the **cardinal ligament**, not at the suspensory ligament
whyNot.C: Runs on the **lateral pelvic wall** toward the obturator canal, away from the ovarian vessels
whyNot.E: Lies **high in the retroperitoneum** at the renal hilum, far above this site

why: The **ureter** passes beneath the **ovarian vessels** in the **suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament**, so clamping or ligating them can injure it. It is also at risk beneath the **uterine artery** in the cardinal ligament (**"water under the bridge"**).

idea.rule: Vessels over the ureter are its danger points: ovarian vessels and uterine artery.
also: Uterine artery crosses over the ureter in the cardinal ligament
Gonadal vessels also cross in front of the ureter in the abdomen
Ovarian vessels run in the suspensory ligament

stem: A 55-year-old woman with uterine prolapse is having a vaginal hysterectomy. The surgeon divides the band that attaches to the cervix, runs posteriorly around the rectum and inserts on the sacrum.
oneliner: 55F + uterine prolapse + vaginal hysterectomy + band from cervix around rectum to sacrum divided → which ligament?

whyNot.A: Runs **forward** from the uterine horn through the inguinal canal to the labia
whyNot.B: Links the **ovary to the uterus**, not to the sacrum
whyNot.D: A peritoneal sheet draped **sideways** from the uterus to the pelvic wall
whyNot.E: Carries **ovarian vessels** from the pelvic brim to the ovary, not to the sacrum

why: The **uterosacral ligament** runs from the **cervix posteriorly** to the **sacrum** and supports the uterus against prolapse. It is divided with the **cardinal ligament** to free the uterus at hysterectomy.

also: Cardinal ligament: uterine artery in its base
Round ligament: anteriorly through inguinal canal
Weak support causes uterine prolapse

stem: A 28-year-old woman has lower abdominal pain and hypotension after a missed period. Ultrasound shows free fluid behind the uterus, and blood is to be aspirated from the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity with a needle passed through the vaginal wall.
oneliner: 28F + missed period + hypotension + free fluid behind uterus + needle aspiration through vaginal wall → which route?
ask: Through which site should the needle pass?

options.D: Anterior vaginal wall near the urethra
options.E: Posterior vaginal wall near the introitus

whyNot.A: Lies in front of the cervix toward the **bladder**; the pouch there is not the **lowest point**
whyNot.C: Leads to the **base of the broad ligament**, beside the **uterine artery and ureter**
whyNot.D: Reaches the **urethra and bladder neck**, below the peritoneum
whyNot.E: Reaches the **rectovaginal septum and perineal body**, below the peritoneal cavity

why: In a standing or supine woman the **rectouterine pouch (of Douglas)** is the **lowest peritoneal recess**, so blood from a **ruptured ectopic pregnancy** collects there. A needle through the **posterior vaginal fornix** reaches it (**culdocentesis**).

idea.rule: Fluid pools in the lowest peritoneal recess: pouch of Douglas in women, rectovesical pouch in men.
also: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy: culdocentesis shows non-clotting blood
Pelvic abscess may collect in the same pouch
Endometriosis often seeds the pouch of Douglas (painful intercourse and defecation)

stem: A 54-year-old woman has ovarian carcinoma that appears confined to one ovary. At staging surgery, the surgeon samples the lymph node group that receives the first spread from this organ.
oneliner: 54F + ovarian carcinoma confined to ovary + first nodal spread → which node group?
ask: Which lymph node group receives the first spread?

whyNot.A: Drain the **vulva, lower vagina** and skin of the perineum, not the ovary
whyNot.B: Drain the **cervix, upper vagina** and other pelvic organs; the ovary's main lymph follows the **ovarian vessels** upward
whyNot.C: Receive the **deep lower limb** and glans; they are not ovarian drainage
whyNot.D: Drain the **distal gut** (hindgut), not the gonad

why: The ovary arises from the **gonadal ridge** near the kidney, so its lymph follows the **gonadal vessels** to the **para-aortic (lumbar) nodes**. The testis drains the same way, not to the inguinal nodes.

idea.rule: Lymph follows the embryonic origin: gonads drain to para-aortic nodes.
also: Testis: para-aortic nodes
Cervix and upper vagina: iliac nodes
Vulva, lower vagina and scrotal skin: superficial inguinal nodes
